newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore PM in new suit vs opposition politician.
newsitem.headline: Singapore PM in new suit vs opposition politician.

text.p: Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong issued a new suit for defamation on Thursday against opposition politician Tang Liang Hong.

A writ of summons posted in the High Court said the suit claimed Workers' Party activist Tang had slandered Goh to, or in the hearing of, Ahmad Osman, a journalist for the pro-government daily Straits Times newspaper, on January 23.
Tang had also libelled Goh in an article written by the same journalist in the newspaper on January 24, the writ said.
The suit is the second brought by the prime minister against Tang since Singapore's general election on January 2.
Tang was an unsuccessful candidate in a hotly contested constituency in the poll, in which the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) won 81 of 83 parliamentary seats.
Tang is also being sued separately for defamation by former prime minister Lee Kuan Yew and nine other members of the PAP for comments he is alleged to have made during the general election campaign.
The January 24 article in the Straits Times quoted Tang giving his views on the earlier defamation suits against him.
The notice in the High Court said Goh was claiming unspecified costs against Tang and gave him eight days to respond to the defamation claims.
A cover note to the writ said it was being posted at the court as a "substituted service", which is used when a defendant is not available to receive a writ in person.

Tang is currently in London and was unavailable for immediate comment. He left Singapore after the election saying he had received death threats, but has said he intends to fight the lawsuits and eventually return to Singapore.
Tang's wife, Teo Siew Har, was cited as a co-defendant in Thursday's writ but was not mentioned in the Straits Times article on January 24 and has shunned media attention.
A Singapore lawyer contacted by Reuters, who declined to be identified, said Teo may have been included in the writ because the court suspected some of Tang's assets were in her name.
The Home Affairs Ministry said on Wednesday it had prevented Teo from leaving Singapore by cancelling all her passports.
It said the Comptroller of Income Tax suspected Teo may have been involved in the administration of Tang's tax matters, which were being investigated by the authorities.
Lawyers acting for Goh and the other plaintiffs were unavailable for immediate comment. Contacted by Reuters, Ahmad said his supervisor had advised him not to discuss the matter.

Lawyers for the PAP leaders obtained a court injunction on Monday to block disposal of assets belonging to Tang and Teo worldwide unless they set aside up to S$11.2 million (US$7.94 million) for possible damages and legal costs.
